questions.stem: Primary sources do <u>not</u> include
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Primary sources include letters, diaries, tax rolls, treaties, tools, clothing, artifacts, graves, paintings, archeological remains…' – materials from the period itself.
Coins from the period are also artifacts. A modern textbook is a later interpretation – a secondary source. Answer: E.
tips: Primary = produced at the time; secondary = written later about it (textbooks, encyclopedias, biographies).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a secondary source?

explanation_steps: Later interpretations are secondary sources.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which one of the following emerged last?
explanation_steps: The textbook's human evolution chart: Australopithecine (the first hominids) → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens (from about 250,000 years ago), which 'gave rise to two distinct subgroups; Neanderthals and Homo sapiens sapiens'.
Neanderthals (100,000–30,000 B.C.E.) are a later subgroup of Homo sapiens, so of the options they emerged last. Answer: A.
tips: Order: australopithecines → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens → Neanderthals / Homo sapiens sapiens.

similar_questions.stem: The first anatomically modern humans ('people like us') were
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The Homo sapiens sapiens… were the first anatomically modern humans.'
Answer: D.

questions.stem: Find the correct chronological sequence of the three stages of human history from 2.5 million to 1200 BCE.
explanation_steps: The textbook: the Paleolithic (Old Stone) Age began about 2.5 million years ago (hunting and gathering); the Neolithic (New Stone) Age from about 8000 B.C.E. brought systematic agriculture; the Bronze Age (about 3000–1200 B.C.E.) followed with metal tools and cities.
Answer: B.
tips: Paleo = old, neo = new: Old Stone → New Stone → Bronze → Iron.

similar_questions.stem: The Neolithic Revolution refers to

options.B: the shift to systematic agriculture and settled villages

explanation_steps: Textbook: the Neolithic Revolution = systematic agriculture and permanent villages.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about Greek philosophy?

options.A: Socrates taught his pupils about love, justice and good behavior.
options.B: Plato believed that the best type of government was republic.
options.C: Aristotle referred to constitutional government as the best one.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Socrates taught his pupils about justice, love, and good behavior' (A true). Aristotle found three good governments – monarchy, aristocracy and constitutional government – 'Aristotle favored the last one' (C true).
Plato wrote The Republic, in which 'the best kind of government is a government headed by philosophers'. Read loosely as 'the government described in The Republic', B is also accepted by the setters.
Since A and C are both true, E cannot be right; the intended answer is D (all of the above).
tips: When two statements are certainly true and there is no 'A and C' option, 'All of the above' is usually intended.

similar_questions.stem: According to Aristotle, the three types of good government were
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'monarchy, aristocracy, and constitutional government. Aristotle favored the last one.'
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Option B is loosely worded: the textbook says Plato's best government was one 'headed by philosophers' (described in his book The Republic), not 'a republic'. A and C are clearly true, so D is keyed. Teacher decision.

questions.stem: Which of the following was <u>not</u> true of Medieval Eritrea?
explanation_steps: The textbook lists the important developments of the medieval period: the Beja expansion and peaceful spread of Islam; Agew immigration; Turkish and Portuguese attempts at conquest in the 16th century; population movements and social change; Tigrean/Amhara expansion.
All four options belong to medieval Eritrea. Answer: E.

questions.stem: Which one of the following was <u>not</u> the political effect of the crusades?

options.A: Some of the Italian states prospered.
options.B: It led to the breakup of feudalism.
options.D: It led to the development of nation-state in Europe.
options.E: It led to the spread of Islam in Europe.

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The Crusades had many effects in Europe. It helped new Italian cities to prosper and strengthened European monarchs'; many nobles died or sold their lands, feudalism weakened and kings gained wealth – 'This paved the way for the development of nation-states.'

questions.stem: Which of the following is <u>not</u> true of the slave trade?

options.A: The Arabs started it to get domestic servants.
options.B: Slavery was also used in some European countries.
options.C: The discovery of sugar plantation increased the demand for slaves.
options.D: Fifteen million Africans were sold between the 16th and 19th centuries.

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'slavery had been practiced in Africa since ancient times… The primary market for African slaves was the land of Arabia, where most slaves were used as domestic servants. Slavery also existed in some European countries' (B true). Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean 'changed dramatically' the demand (C true). 'As many as 12 to 15 million' were taken (D roughly true).
The Arabs were the main market, but they did not start the slave trade – slavery already existed in Africa since ancient times. Answer: A.
tips: Read the exact claim: 'started it' is stronger than 'were the main market'.

questions.stem: Describe the following terms briefly: 2.1 Bevin–Sforza Plan  2.2 Truman Doctrine (2 points)
questions.answer: 2.1 Bevin–Sforza Plan: a secret 1949 agreement between the British foreign minister Ernest Bevin and the Italian foreign minister Carlo Sforza to divide the former Italian colonies – Eritrea to be partitioned between Ethiopia (highlands and coast) and the Sudan (western lowlands), Italy to get trusteeship over Somalia and Tripolitania; the UN General Assembly rejected it (May 1949). 2.2 Truman Doctrine: US President Truman's 1947 policy of giving economic and military aid to countries (first Greece and Turkey) threatened by communism – the start of 'containment'.
explanation_steps: The textbook (11.3): the Bevin–Sforza plan proposed partitioning Eritrea between Ethiopia and the Sudan; it was defeated at the UN and led Eritrean parties to form the Independence Bloc.
The textbook (12.1): 'the Truman Doctrine… the United States would provide money to countries that were threatened by communist expansion' – Greece and Turkey.
marking_points: 1 point: Bevin–Sforza = 1949 British–Italian plan to partition Eritrea between Ethiopia and Sudan (rejected by the UN)
1 point: Truman Doctrine = 1947 US aid to countries (Greece, Turkey) resisting communism / containment
tips: Name who, when, and what each plan did in one sentence.

questions.stem: Give any <u>two</u> of the positive effects of Italian colonial rule in Eritrea. (2 points)
questions.answer: Any two of: modern infrastructure (roads, the Massawa–Asmara–Keren–Agordat railway, the Asmara–Massawa cableway, ports); growth of towns (urbanisation, e.g. Asmara); introduction of industries and factories and a class of Eritrean workers; creation of a single territory with defined boundaries and a centralised modern administration, which laid the basis of Eritrean national identity.
explanation_steps: The textbook describes the Italian colonial economy: the railway from Massawa to Asmara and beyond, roads and the cableway, the growth of Asmara, light industries (especially in the 1930s), and wage labour.
It also stresses that colonialism created Eritrea as a single territory with fixed boundaries – the basis of the later Eritrean identity.
marking_points: 1 point each for any two: infrastructure (roads, railway, cableway, ports); urbanisation; industries/wage labour; unified territory, boundaries and modern administration.
tips: 'Positive' = unintended benefits: infrastructure, towns, industry, unified territory.
